items.title: Ext via an injective resolution of the second variable
items.strategy: Fix supplied injective resolution data and define the cochain complex Hom(M,I(N)), including its degree and differential convention; define Ext_I^n(M,N) as its cohomology.

items.title: Ext via a projective resolution of the first variable
items.strategy: Fix supplied projective resolution data and define the Hom cochain complex Hom(P(M),N), explicitly stating the contravariant differential sign; define Ext_P^n(M,N) as its cohomology.

items.title: The degree-zero injective construction of Ext is Hom
items.strategy: Identify H^0 Hom(M,I(N)) with Hom(M,N) using the initial monomorphism into the injective resolution and left exactness; retain both-variable naturality.

items.title: The degree-zero projective construction of Ext is Hom
items.strategy: Identify H^0 Hom(P(M),N) with Hom(M,N) using the augmentation of the projective resolution and the exactness of the augmented Hom sequence.

items.title: Injective-resolution Ext has the stated bifunctor variance
items.strategy: Use precomposition directly for the first variable and the supplied injective comparison extension for the second; show homotopic comparisons give the same cohomology map.

items.title: Projective-resolution Ext has the stated bifunctor variance
items.strategy: Use postcomposition for the second variable and the contravariant projective comparison lift for the first; pass to cohomology through comparison homotopy independence.

items.title: Positive injective-resolution Ext vanishes on an injective second variable
items.strategy: Use the length-zero injective resolution of an injective object, so its Hom cochain complex is concentrated in degree zero.

items.title: Positive projective-resolution Ext vanishes on a projective first variable
items.strategy: Use the length-zero projective resolution of a projective object, so its Hom cochain complex is concentrated in degree zero.

items.title: The Hom double complex of projective and injective resolutions
items.strategy: For fixed M and N define K^{p,q}=Hom(P_p(M),I^q(N)), state the horizontal contravariant and vertical covariant differentials, and fix first-quadrant indexing.

items.title: The two Hom double-complex differentials commute before signing
items.strategy: Compute both composites on a homogeneous map and use d_P d_P=0 and d_I d_I=0; choose the total sign from the horizontal degree so the signed total differential squares to zero.

items.title: The direct-sum total complex on finite diagonals
items.strategy: Define Tot^n K as the direct sum over p+q=n, record the signed differential, and state why first-quadrant finite diagonals eliminate sum-versus-product ambiguity.

items.title: Acyclic assembly by exact columns
items.strategy: Filter finite diagonal truncations by columns and repeatedly use short exact sequences to show that an augmented exact-column edge complex maps quasi-isomorphically to Tot; do not invoke a spectral sequence.

items.title: Acyclic assembly by exact rows
items.strategy: Apply the same finite-truncation proof after interchanging rows and columns, retaining the stated augmentation orientation.

items.title: Hom from a projective makes injective-resolution columns exact
items.strategy: For each projective P_p, apply exactness of Hom(P_p,-) to the augmented injective resolution of N and identify the resulting column and its edge.

items.title: Hom into an injective makes projective-resolution rows exact
items.strategy: For each injective I^q, apply exactness of Hom(-,I^q) to the augmented projective resolution of M and identify the resulting row and its edge.

items.title: Projective and injective constructions of Ext are naturally isomorphic
items.strategy: Compare the two augmented edge Hom complexes with Tot Hom(P,I). The exact-column and exact-row assembly lemmas yield two quasi-isomorphisms, hence a cohomology isomorphism; retain the comparison maps for later naturality.

items.title: The Ext balance isomorphism is independent of resolution comparison data
items.strategy: View both constructions as universal cohomological delta functors extending Hom and use degree-zero uniqueness to identify the total-complex comparison with the unique balance map.

items.title: The Ext balance isomorphism is natural in both variables
items.strategy: Use functorial projective and injective comparison maps to make the two edge-to-total maps commute, then apply cohomology and the independence lemma.

items.title: Ext balance isomorphisms satisfy change-of-resolution cocycle laws
items.strategy: Compose comparison maps through a third resolution and use uniqueness of the universal-delta extension to prove the identity and composition laws.

items.title: The balanced Ext bifunctor
items.strategy: After the comparison, independence, naturality, and cocycle results, define Ext^n_A(-,-) to denote either construction and list those results as the justification for the notation.

items.title: The long exact Ext sequence in the second variable
items.strategy: Use the cohomological delta-functor structure of the injective construction, replace it by balanced Ext, and print the connecting morphisms and their naturality in both the short exact sequence and M.

items.title: The long exact Ext sequence in the first variable
items.strategy: Use the homological delta-functor structure of the projective construction on the opposite category, translate the variance carefully, and print the declared connecting-arrow sign.

items.title: The two Ext long exact sequences agree under balance
items.strategy: Use the natural balance isomorphism as a morphism of universal delta functors, so its squares with all connecting morphisms commute.

items.title: Ext dimension shifting in the first variable
items.strategy: Identify the truncated projective-resolution tail with a resolution of the first syzygy; state the separate low-degree exact segment before the natural isomorphisms for q at least one.

items.title: Ext dimension shifting in the second variable
items.strategy: Apply the second-variable long exact sequence to an injective copresentation 0 -> N -> I -> Sigma N -> 0 and use positive Ext-vanishing of I.

items.title: Ext can be computed from any projective resolution of the first variable
items.strategy: Use the projective construction together with its comparison-homotopy independence and the balanced definition to remove dependence on the supplied choice.

items.title: Ext can be computed from any injective resolution of the second variable
items.strategy: Use the injective construction together with injective comparison-homotopy independence and the balanced definition to remove dependence on the supplied choice.

items.title: Exact functors compatible with Hom transport Ext under stated adjunction hypotheses
items.strategy: State an exact functor and its indicated adjoint Hom-identification, require the stated preservation of projectives or injectives, transport the selected resolution, and identify the resulting Hom complexes; do not assert generic categorical functoriality of Ext.

items.title: Ext one of Z modulo n by Z is Z modulo n
items.strategy: Apply Hom(-,Z) to 0 -> Z --n--> Z -> Z/n -> 0. Its cokernel is Z/n, so Ext^1_Z(Z/n,Z) is nonzero for n greater than one.

items.title: FALSE: Ext is defined before choosing or supplying resolutions
items.strategy: The two constructions require supplied projective or injective resolution data; balance later compares their results but does not supply missing data.

items.title: FALSE: projective and injective Ext are equal by definition
items.strategy: They arise from different Hom complexes. Their equality is the natural isomorphism furnished by the double-complex and assembly proof.

items.title: FALSE: Ext is covariant in both variables
items.strategy: Precomposition reverses arrows in the first variable while postcomposition preserves them in the second; cite the two constructed variance laws.

items.title: FALSE: positive Ext vanishes whenever either variable is injective
items.strategy: The vanishing inputs are an injective second variable or a projective first variable. Give a cyclic-group countercalculation in the examples page for the reversed injective claim.

items.title: FALSE: double-complex totalisation is unambiguous with infinite diagonals
items.strategy: The proof uses a first-quadrant complex precisely so every total-degree diagonal is finite; outside that setting direct-sum and product totalisations can differ.

items.title: FALSE: balance of Ext requires spectral-sequence pages
items.strategy: The finite-diagonal acyclic-assembly lemmas directly compare both edge complexes with Tot and contain no spectral-sequence appeal.

items.title: Ext zero as Hom in both constructions
items.strategy: Write the degree-zero identifications in the projective and injective complexes and compare them through balanced Ext.

items.title: Ext from a two-term projective resolution
items.strategy: Apply Hom(-,N) to a displayed two-term projective resolution and identify Ext^0 and Ext^1 as its kernel and cokernel, with higher groups zero.

items.title: Ext of a cyclic abelian group by an abelian group
items.strategy: Use the resolution 0 -> Z --n--> Z -> Z/n -> 0 to calculate Ext^1_Z(Z/n,A)=A/nA and show the higher terms vanish.

items.title: The Hom double complex in low bidegrees
items.strategy: Display K^{0,0}, K^{1,0}, K^{0,1}, and K^{1,1}, label the two unsigned differentials, and compute the signed total differential in degrees zero and one.

items.title: An Ext dimension shift
items.strategy: Use the displayed cyclic-group projective presentation to identify Ext^{n+1}(M,N) with Ext^n(Omega M,N), distinguishing the low-degree exact segment.

items.title: Positive Ext need not vanish for an injective first variable
items.strategy: Use Q/Z as an injective abelian group in the first variable and calculate a nonzero Ext^1 against a suitable second variable, separating the correct variance from the false symmetry.

items.title: Naturality of the balance isomorphism
items.strategy: For maps M' -> M and N -> N' draw the square of projective and injective Ext computations and verify that both routes agree through the total-complex comparison.

items.title: An extension of an object by an object in an abelian category
items.strategy: Define an extension of M by N to be a short exact sequence 0 -> N -> E -> M -> 0, explicitly fixing the order used by Ext^1(M,N).

items.title: Equivalence of extensions
items.strategy: Define an equivalence as a morphism of short exact sequences inducing the identity on the subobject N and quotient M.

items.title: A morphism of extensions is an isomorphism
items.strategy: Apply the categorical short five lemma to the two short exact rows with identity outer maps.

items.title: Equivalence of extensions is an equivalence relation
items.strategy: Use identity and composition for reflexivity and transitivity; use the inverse from the previous proposition for symmetry.

items.title: The split extension class
items.strategy: Define the distinguished class by 0 -> N -> N direct-sum M -> M -> 0 and use an equivalence to show every split extension represents it.

items.title: Pullback and pushout of an extension
items.strategy: Use the published pullback and pushout universal properties to define pullback in the quotient variable and pushout in the subobject variable, recording the induced short exact sequences.

items.title: Pullback and pushout descend to extension classes
items.strategy: Map a representative equivalence through the relevant universal square and use the short five lemma to obtain an equivalence of the induced extensions.

items.title: The Baer sum of extension classes
items.strategy: Take the direct sum of two extensions, pull it back along the diagonal M -> M direct-sum M, then push it out along the codiagonal N direct-sum N -> N.

items.title: The Baer sum is independent of representatives
items.strategy: Apply functoriality of direct sum, then the descent lemma for the diagonal pullback and codiagonal pushout, to an equivalence of each input extension.

items.title: Baer sum makes extension classes an abelian group
items.strategy: Use biproduct coherence to prove associativity and commutativity; identify the split class as zero and push out along minus the identity of N for inverses.

items.title: Extension classes are contravariant in the quotient and covariant in the subobject
items.strategy: Use pullback along maps of quotient objects and pushout along maps of subobjects; prove that the induced maps preserve the Baer group law.

items.title: The derived Ext-one class of an extension
items.strategy: Apply the second-variable long exact Ext sequence to the extension and define its class as the connecting image of the identity of M.

items.title: Equivalent extensions have the same Ext class
items.strategy: Apply naturality of the connecting morphism to a morphism of short exact sequences which is the identity at both endpoints.

items.title: Every Ext-one class is represented by an extension
items.strategy: Represent a class by a map from the first syzygy into N, then push out the first projective syzygy sequence along that map and identify its connecting class.

items.title: Two extensions with the same Ext class are equivalent
items.strategy: Compare both extensions with the common pushout model from a projective presentation; equality of connecting classes supplies the map which gives the identity-endpoint equivalence.

items.title: Yoneda Ext one is naturally isomorphic to derived Ext one
items.strategy: Use the two preceding lemmas for bijectivity, verify compatibility with Baer sum through diagonal-pullback and codiagonal-pushout, and use long-exact naturality for both variables.

items.title: Extension classes form a set whenever derived Ext one does
items.strategy: Transfer sethood across the established bijection, retaining the locally small and essentially small hypotheses rather than forming an unchecked proper-class quotient.

items.title: An n-fold Yoneda extension
items.strategy: Define an n-fold extension of M by N as an exact sequence 0 -> N -> E_(n-1) -> ... -> E_0 -> M -> 0.

items.title: Equivalence of n-fold extensions
items.strategy: Define the equivalence relation generated by chain maps that are the identity at the two ends, emphasizing that a single middle-term isomorphism is not required for n greater than one.

items.title: The Yoneda splice product
items.strategy: Concatenate a p-fold extension of L by N with a q-fold extension of M by L and record the resulting order and degree p+q.

items.title: Yoneda splicing is well-defined on equivalence classes
items.strategy: Splice a generating chain map on either factor with identities on the other, then pass to the generated equivalence relation.

items.title: The Yoneda product is associative and unital
items.strategy: Associativity is literal associativity of concatenation up to the stated equivalence; extend degree zero by Hom and use identity extensions as two-sided units.

items.title: Higher Yoneda Ext agrees with derived Ext
items.strategy: Under enough projectives or enough injectives and the stated smallness condition, dimension-shift n-extensions down to Ext one and compare the resulting class with derived Ext by induction.

items.title: The Yoneda product agrees with derived Ext composition
items.strategy: Track the connecting classes of two extensions through the dimension-shift comparison and show that concatenation induces the shifted composition in derived Ext.

items.title: The graded Ext algebra of an object
items.strategy: Define Ext-star(M,M) with the Yoneda product and state only associativity and the degree-zero identity unit, not graded commutativity.

items.title: Projective dimension of an object
items.strategy: Define projective dimension as the least length of a projective resolution, or infinity when no finite such resolution exists, relative to enough projectives or supplied resolution data.

items.title: Injective dimension of an object
items.strategy: Define injective dimension dually as the least length of an injective resolution, or infinity, with the same existence qualification.

items.title: Projective dimension at most n iff the nth syzygy is projective
items.strategy: For n at least one, truncate in one direction and iterate Schanuel in the other to make projectivity independent of the selected resolution.

items.title: Projective dimension at most n iff higher Ext vanishes
items.strategy: Treat n=0 directly, and for n at least one use dimension shifting and the syzygy criterion; derive the Ext-one projectivity test from the first projective-resolution stage.

items.title: Injective dimension at most n iff higher Ext vanishes
items.strategy: Apply the dual cosyzygy and second-variable dimension-shifting argument to characterize injective dimension by Ext in the second variable.

items.title: Finite projective dimension is the largest nonzero Ext degree
items.strategy: For a nonzero object with a witness object and the stated enough-projectives and smallness hypotheses, combine the least-length criterion with the vanishing theorem; state separately the zero-object convention.

items.title: Left and right global dimension of a ring
items.strategy: Define the two numbers as the respective suprema of projective dimensions of left and right modules and explicitly keep their handedness separate.

items.title: Global dimension of an abelian category
items.strategy: Define the supremum of projective dimensions when enough projectives are supplied, and reserve an injective formulation for the later theorem that gives its hypotheses.

items.title: Global dimension is the supremum of nonzero Ext degrees
items.strategy: Take suprema in the projective- and injective-dimension vanishing characterizations and retain the stated enough-projectives or enough-injectives assumptions.

items.title: Global dimension zero characterises semisimple module categories
items.strategy: Use the published equivalence between semisimplicity, splitting, and every module being projective, then translate length-zero resolutions into global dimension zero.

items.title: Hereditary rings have global dimension at most one
items.strategy: State the left hypothesis that every submodule of a projective left module is projective and its right-handed dual; apply it to the first syzygy of every module.

items.title: Subgroups of free abelian groups are free
items.strategy: Prove the infinite-rank form by well-ordering a basis, filtering the subgroup by the induced free summands, and adjoining at each successor a cyclic direct summand using the PID submodule theorem; take unions at limit stages.

items.title: The integers have global dimension one
items.strategy: Use the preceding subgroup-freeness lemma to make every first syzygy of a free presentation projective, obtaining global dimension at most one; use the nonzero Ext^1 of Z/n by Z for the lower bound.

items.title: FALSE: an extension of M by N represents Ext one of N by M
items.strategy: The displayed exact sequence puts N in the subobject position and M in the quotient position, hence represents Ext^1(M,N).

items.title: FALSE: Baer sum only takes the direct sum of middle objects
items.strategy: The direct sum is only an intermediate extension; the diagonal pullback and codiagonal pushout are required to restore the fixed endpoints.

items.title: FALSE: extension classes automatically form a set
items.strategy: A quotient of a class has not been shown small merely by naming it; the Ext-one comparison supplies sethood under its explicit hypotheses.

items.title: FALSE: the Yoneda product is graded commutative for every abelian category
items.strategy: Splicing yields an associative product, but no symmetric interchange is available in an arbitrary abelian category; the page makes no graded-commutativity claim.

items.title: FALSE: projective dimension is the length of any projective resolution
items.strategy: It is the least possible finite length; one may always prolong a resolution, and the syzygy criterion detects the minimum.

items.title: FALSE: left and right global dimensions are equal by definition
items.strategy: The definitions take separate suprema over left and right modules. Equality, when true under extra hypotheses, is a theorem rather than notation.

title: Yoneda Extensions and Homological Dimension — Examples

items.title: The split extension as the zero Baer class
items.strategy: Compute the Baer sum of a split extension with an arbitrary extension and exhibit the induced equivalence with the original representative.

items.title: Baer sum of two extensions of cyclic groups
items.strategy: Use representatives of extensions of Z/n by Z/m, form their direct sum, and explicitly carry out the diagonal pullback and codiagonal pushout.

items.title: Ext one of Z modulo n by an abelian group as extension classes
items.strategy: Combine the cyclic Ext calculation with the Yoneda Ext-one theorem to interpret A/nA as equivalence classes of extensions of Z/n by A.

items.title: Splicing two short exact sequences
items.strategy: Concatenate two displayed short exact sequences with common middle endpoint and identify the resulting two-fold extension and its derived Ext product.

items.title: A noncommutative Yoneda product
items.strategy: Use a finite-dimensional algebra with composable nonsymmetric extension classes to calculate two products in opposite orders and show they differ or one is undefined by endpoints.

items.title: Projective dimension of a cyclic abelian group
items.strategy: Use 0 -> Z --n--> Z -> Z/n -> 0 and the nonzero Ext^1 calculation to prove that Z/n has projective dimension one over Z.

items.title: Global dimension of a field and of the integers
items.strategy: Every vector space is free, giving global dimension zero for a field; pair the cyclic-group witness with the subgroup-freeness argument for global dimension one of Z.

items.title: Equivalent higher extensions need not have one middle-term isomorphism
items.strategy: Give a zigzag of endpoint-identity chain maps between two two-fold extensions whose middle-object shapes prevent a single isomorphism, illustrating the generated equivalence relation.
